title: Two parts of the national territory (Art. I)
ask: Under Art. I, what are the two parts of the national territory?
items: The Philippine archipelago, with all the islands and waters embraced therein
All other territories over which the Philippines has sovereignty or jurisdiction
src: Art. I

title: Domains and submarine areas named in Art. I
ask: Art. I says the territory consists of three domains and includes five maritime/submarine areas. Name all eight, in order.
items: Terrestrial domain
Fluvial domain
Aerial domain
Territorial sea
Seabed
Subsoil
Insular shelves
Other submarine areas
src: Art. I

title: Archipelagic doctrine and straight baselines
ask: State the elements of the archipelagic doctrine and the straight baseline method.
items: Islands and the waters around them form one integrated unit (unity of land and water)
Waters around, between and connecting the islands are internal waters
This holds ‘regardless of their breadth and dimensions’ (Art. I, last sentence)
Straight baselines join appropriate points of the outermost islands
The lines may not depart to any appreciable extent from the general direction of the coast
Waters landward of the baselines are internal (archipelagic) waters; zones are measured outward from the baselines
src: Art. I; RA 9522; Magallona

title: Modes of acquiring or losing territory
ask: What are the four modes by which a State acquires or loses territory (Magallona)?
items: Occupation
Accretion
Cession
Prescription
src: Magallona v. Ermita

title: UNCLOS maritime zones and their breadths
ask: List the UNCLOS maritime zones, from the baselines outward, with their breadths.
items: Internal/archipelagic waters: landward of the baselines
Territorial sea: 12 nautical miles from the baselines
Contiguous zone: 24 nautical miles from the baselines (12 beyond the territorial sea)
Exclusive economic zone: 200 nautical miles from the baselines
Continental shelf: natural prolongation to the margin’s edge, or 200 nm if the margin is shorter
Continental shelf outer limit: never beyond 350 nm (or 100 nm from the 2,500-m isobath)
High seas: beyond the EEZ, open to all States

title: What the coastal State holds in each zone
ask: For each maritime zone, what rights does the coastal State have?
items: Internal/archipelagic waters: sovereignty, subject to innocent passage and archipelagic sea lanes passage
Territorial sea: sovereignty (including airspace, bed, subsoil), subject to innocent passage of ships
Contiguous zone: control to prevent and punish infringement of customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws
EEZ: sovereign rights to explore, exploit, conserve and manage living and non-living resources
EEZ: jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research, and the marine environment
Continental shelf: exclusive sovereign rights over seabed and subsoil resources
Territory is sovereignty; zones beyond the territorial sea give only sovereign rights and jurisdiction
src: UNCLOS Arts. 2, 17, 33, 56, 77; Magallona; 2016 Award

title: Archipelagic baseline limits (why KIG was left out)
ask: What limits does UNCLOS Art. 47 put on archipelagic baselines, and how did they shape RA 9522?
items: Water-to-land ratio inside the baselines must be between 1:1 and 9:1
Each baseline may not exceed 100 nm; up to 3% of them may reach 125 nm
Baselines must not depart appreciably from the general configuration of the archipelago
Enclosing the KIG and Scarborough would breach these limits, so RA 9522 left them out
Instead they are a ‘regime of islands’ (UNCLOS Art. 121), with the claim preserved
src: UNCLOS Art. 47; RA 9522, Sec. 2; Magallona

title: Why RA 9522 is valid (Magallona)
ask: Give the reasons Magallona upheld RA 9522 (the baselines law).
items: UNCLOS regulates sea-use rights and maritime zones; it is not a mode of acquiring territory
Baselines laws neither add to nor reduce Philippine territory
RA 9522 is only a statutory tool to demarcate the maritime zones and continental shelf
Classifying KIG and Scarborough as a ‘regime of islands’ does not cede them
Archipelagic waters stay under Philippine sovereignty despite innocent and sea lanes passage
Those passage rights already bind the Philippines under international law
src: Magallona v. Ermita (2011)

title: Classifying maritime features (UNCLOS Art. 121)
ask: How are maritime features classified, and what entitlements does each get?
items: Island: naturally formed land, surrounded by water, above water at high tide
Fully entitled island (sustains human habitation or economic life of its own): territorial sea, contiguous zone, EEZ, continental shelf
Rock (cannot sustain habitation or economic life of its own): no EEZ or continental shelf; 12-nm territorial sea
Low-tide elevation (above water only at low tide): no territorial sea of its own; cannot be appropriated
Submerged feature: part of the seabed; no entitlement
Artificial island: no territorial sea; reclamation never upgrades a feature
Features are judged in their natural condition; outside supplies do not count
src: UNCLOS Arts. 13, 60, 121; South China Sea Arbitration (2016)

title: South China Sea Award: main findings
ask: What did the 2016 South China Sea Award decide on entitlements?
items: China’s nine-dash-line historic rights have no legal basis beyond UNCLOS entitlements
Any historic rights were extinguished to the extent incompatible with UNCLOS
No Spratly feature is a fully entitled island; none generates an EEZ
The Spratlys cannot generate an EEZ collectively as a unit
Scarborough Shoal and Itu Aba are rocks; Mischief Reef and Second Thomas Shoal are low-tide elevations in the PH EEZ
It did NOT decide sovereignty over any feature, nor delimit boundaries
src: In re South China Sea Arbitration (July 12, 2016)

title: China’s violations found in the Award
ask: What UNCLOS violations by China did the 2016 Award find?
items: Violated Philippine sovereign rights in its EEZ (fishing and petroleum exploration)
Prevented Filipino traditional fishing at Scarborough Shoal
Harmed the marine environment by reclamation at seven Spratly features and tolerating harmful harvesting
Created a serious risk of collision by obstructing Philippine vessels at Scarborough (2012)
src: South China Sea Arbitration (2016)

title: Why the MOA-AD was unconstitutional (North Cotabato)
ask: Why was the MOA-AD struck down, and what may the President do in peace talks?
items: The ‘Bangsamoro Juridical Entity’ had associative status, which presupposes a State
The Executive guaranteed constitutional amendments it has no power to deliver
The panel did not consult affected LGUs and indigenous peoples: grave abuse
Decided despite mootness because of grave constitutional issues
Peace power is implied from her powers as Chief Executive and Commander-in-Chief
She may recommend amendments to Congress, but not implement them unilaterally
src: Province of North Cotabato v. GRP Peace Panel (2008)

title: Citizens of the Philippines (Art. IV, Sec. 1)
ask: Who are the four classes of citizens of the Philippines under Art. IV, Sec. 1?
items: Those who are citizens of the Philippines at the time of the adoption of this Constitution
Those whose fathers or mothers are citizens of the Philippines
Those born before January 17, 1973, of Filipino mothers, who elect Philippine citizenship upon reaching the age of majority
Those who are naturalized in accordance with law
src: Art. IV, Sec. 1

title: Art. IV, Secs. 2–5 in one line each
ask: State the rule of each of Art. IV, Secs. 2 to 5.
items: Sec. 2: natural-born are citizens from birth without any act to acquire or perfect citizenship
Sec. 2: those who elect under Sec. 1(3) are deemed natural-born
Sec. 3: citizenship may be lost or reacquired in the manner provided by law
Sec. 4: citizens who marry aliens retain citizenship unless, by act or omission, deemed under law to have renounced it
Sec. 5: dual allegiance is inimical to the national interest and shall be dealt with by law
src: Art. IV, Secs. 2–5

title: Who is natural-born
ask: Who are natural-born citizens under the Constitution and the cases?
items: Citizens from birth by blood (jus sanguinis), needing no act to acquire or perfect citizenship
Those who elect under Art. IV, Sec. 1(3): deemed natural-born
Illegitimate child of a Filipino father, once filiation is proved (Tecson)
Foundlings found in the Philippines (David v. SET; RA 11767)
Natural-born Filipinos who reacquire by repatriation or RA 9225: status restored (Bengson; David)
Only two kinds exist: natural-born and naturalized; whoever is not naturalized is natural-born (Bengson)
src: Art. IV, Secs. 1–2; Tecson; David v. SET; Bengson

title: Why foundlings are natural-born (David v. SET)
ask: What are the bases in David v. SET for treating foundlings as natural-born?
items: The 1934–35 framers never intended to exclude foundlings
High statistical probability that a child found here has Filipino parents
Generally accepted principle: a foundling is presumed born of nationals of the State where found
Sources: 1930 Hague Convention, Art. 14; 1961 Statelessness Convention, Art. 2
Binding through incorporation (Art. II, Sec. 2) even without ratification
Now by statute: RA 11767 (2022) presumes foundlings natural-born
src: David v. SET (2016)

title: How FPJ was Filipino (Tecson chain)
ask: Trace the chain by which FPJ was a Filipino in Tecson.
items: Lorenzo Pou, a Spanish subject presumed resident here, died in Pangasinan (1954)
He became Filipino by mass naturalization under the Philippine Bill of 1902
His citizenship passed to his son Allan F. Poe
FPJ’s filiation to Allan was shown by his birth certificate
The 1935 ‘father is a citizen’ rule makes no distinction by legitimacy
src: Tecson v. COMELEC (2004)

title: Offices requiring natural-born citizenship
ask: Which offices does the Constitution reserve for natural-born citizens?
items: President and Vice President (Art. VII, Secs. 2–3)
Senators and Members of the House (Art. VI, Secs. 3 and 6)
Justices of the Supreme Court and any lower collegiate court (Art. VIII, Sec. 7(1))
Members of the CSC, COMELEC and COA (Art. IX-B, C, D, Sec. 1)
Ombudsman and his Deputies (Art. XI, Sec. 8)
Monetary Board members (Art. XII, Sec. 20)
Commission on Human Rights members (Art. XIII, Sec. 17(2))
By law, not Constitution: RTC and first-level judges (BP 129); local officials need only citizenship
src: Arts. VI–IX, XI–XIII; BP 129; LGC, Sec. 39

title: Election of citizenship: requisites
ask: What are the requisites for a valid election of Philippine citizenship under Art. IV, Sec. 1(3) and CA 625?
items: Born before January 17, 1973
Of a Filipino mother (and alien father)
Elects upon reaching the age of majority
A statement of election signed and sworn before an officer authorized to administer oaths
An oath of allegiance to the Constitution and Government of the Philippines
Both filed/registered with the nearest civil registry
Within a reasonable time after majority: generally three years (Sagun)
No judicial declaration: election is a private act, not a court proceeding (Sagun)
src: Art. IV, Sec. 1(3); CA 625, Sec. 1; Republic v. Sagun

title: Implied election (Co v. HRET)
ask: Which acts count as implied election of citizenship under Co v. HRET, and for whom?
items: Voting in elections
Holding a public office where citizenship is a qualification
Practising a profession open only to Filipinos
Only for those already treated as Filipino when the time to elect came
It does not cure a late or unregistered formal election (Sagun)
src: Co v. HRET (1991); Republic v. Sagun (2012)

title: Which body decides a candidate’s citizenship
ask: Which body decides a candidate’s or official’s citizenship at each stage?
items: Before the election (COC stage): COMELEC, on a petition to deny due course or cancel the COC
Sitting or proclaimed Member of the House: HRET (Co v. HRET)
Sitting or proclaimed Senator: SET (David v. SET)
President or Vice President after the election: PET (Tecson)
The Supreme Court reviews these tribunals only for grave abuse
src: Art. VI, Sec. 17; Art. VII, Sec. 4; Tecson; David v. SET; Co v. HRET

title: Modes of naturalization
ask: What are the modes of naturalization (the three main modes plus derivative and historical ones)?
items: Judicial: petition in court under CA 473 (Revised Naturalization Law)
Administrative: RA 9139, before the Special Committee on Naturalization (chaired by the Solicitor General)
Legislative: a special law of Congress (naturalized, not natural-born)
Derivative: minor children of a naturalized father (CA 473, Sec. 15; Tan Co)
Historical: mass naturalization of resident Spanish subjects (Philippine Bill of 1902)
Historical: administrative naturalization under LOI 270 for a limited period
src: CA 473; RA 9139; Philippine Bill of 1902; LOI 270; Tan Co

title: CA 473 qualifications (judicial naturalization)
ask: What are the six qualifications for judicial naturalization under CA 473, Sec. 2?
items: At least 21 years old on the day of the hearing
Continuous residence in the Philippines for at least 10 years
Good moral character; believes in the Constitution; proper and irreproachable conduct
Real estate worth at least ₱5,000, or a known lucrative trade, profession or lawful occupation
Speaks and writes English or Spanish and one principal Philippine language
Has enrolled minor children of school age in schools teaching Philippine history, government and civics
src: CA 473, Sec. 2; Mahtani (lucrative = appreciable margin of income over expenses)

title: When 10 years’ residence is cut to 5 (CA 473, Sec. 3)
ask: In what five cases is the 10-year residence requirement reduced to five years under CA 473, Sec. 3?
items: Has held office in the Philippine government or a political subdivision
Established a new industry or introduced a useful invention in the Philippines
Married to a Filipino woman
Taught for at least two years in a public or recognized private school not limited to one nationality
Born in the Philippines
src: CA 473, Sec. 3

title: Disqualifications for naturalization
ask: Who are disqualified from naturalization (CA 473, Sec. 4; substantially the same in RA 9139, Sec. 4)?
items: Those opposed to organized government or affiliated with groups teaching such doctrines
Those defending or teaching the necessity of violence, personal assault or assassination for their ideas
Polygamists or believers in polygamy
Those convicted of a crime involving moral turpitude
Those suffering from mental alienation or an incurable contagious disease
Those who have not mingled socially with Filipinos or embraced their customs, traditions and ideals
Citizens of a nation at war with the Philippines, during the war
Citizens of a country whose laws do not let Filipinos naturalize there
src: CA 473, Sec. 4; RA 9139, Sec. 4

title: CA 473 strict-compliance requirements
ask: What procedural requirements of CA 473 are strictly enforced (Go, Go Pei Hung)?
items: Declaration of intention filed one year before the petition
Excused if born here and schooled here, or resident for 30 years
Certificate of arrival must be attached; never excused (Go Pei Hung)
Petition must state all former residences; omission is jurisdictional (Go)
Two credible witnesses of good standing with personal knowledge of the applicant (Go)
Naturalization is a privilege, strictly construed against the applicant
src: CA 473, Secs. 5–7; Go v. Republic; Republic v. Go Pei Hung

title: Before a naturalization grant becomes executory (RA 530)
ask: Under RA 530, what must the applicant show during the two years after the decision before taking the oath?
items: Has not left the Philippines
Has dedicated himself continuously to a lawful calling or profession
Has not been convicted of any offense or violation of government rules
Has not committed any act prejudicial to the nation or contrary to announced government policies
Only then, after hearing, does he take the oath and receive the certificate
src: RA 530, Sec. 1 (amending CA 473)

title: RA 9139 qualifications (administrative naturalization)
ask: What are the qualifications for administrative naturalization under RA 9139, Sec. 3?
items: Born in the Philippines and residing here since birth
At least 18 years old when the petition is filed
Good moral character; believes in the Constitution; irreproachable conduct
Primary and secondary schooling where Philippine history, government and civics are taught, open to all races
Minor children of school age enrolled in similar schools
A known trade, business, profession or lawful occupation with income sufficient for self and family
Able to read, write and speak Filipino or any Philippine dialect
Has mingled with Filipinos and sincerely desires to embrace their customs, traditions and ideals
src: RA 9139, Sec. 3

title: Judicial (CA 473) versus administrative (RA 9139) naturalization
ask: Contrast judicial naturalization under CA 473 with administrative naturalization under RA 9139.
items: Forum: regional trial court vs. Special Committee on Naturalization
Who: any qualified alien vs. only aliens born and residing here since birth
Minimum age: 21 vs. 18
Residence: 10 years (5 in some cases) vs. since birth
Means: ₱5,000 real estate or lucrative occupation vs. income sufficient for self and family
Language: English or Spanish plus a principal Philippine language vs. Filipino or any dialect
Declaration of intention one year ahead: required (unless excused) vs. none

title: Grounds for losing citizenship (CA 63)
ask: What are the grounds for losing Philippine citizenship under CA 63, Sec. 1?
items: Naturalization in a foreign country
Express renunciation of citizenship
Oath of allegiance to support the constitution or laws of a foreign country (at 21 or older)
Rendering service to, or accepting a commission in, foreign armed forces (with exceptions)
Cancellation of the certificate of naturalization
Being declared a deserter of the Philippine armed forces in wartime (unless pardoned or amnestied)
Old ground (marriage of a Filipino woman to a foreigner) no longer applies: Art. IV, Sec. 4
src: CA 63, Sec. 1, as amended by RA 106; Art. IV, Sec. 4

title: Proving loss of citizenship (Aznar; Willie Yu)
ask: How is loss of citizenship proved, and what is not enough?
items: Loss is not presumed; one born of a Filipino parent is presumed to stay Filipino
The challenger must prove a CA 63 ground
An alien certificate of registration or foreign certification is not renunciation; at most dual citizenship (Aznar)
Express renunciation: made known distinctly and explicitly (Willie Yu)
Conduct can be express renunciation: using a foreign passport and declaring foreign nationality (Willie Yu)
Contrast Frivaldo and Labo (1989): naturalization abroad was proved
src: Aznar v. COMELEC (1990); Willie Yu v. Defensor-Santiago (1989)

title: Modes of reacquiring citizenship
ask: What are the modes of reacquiring Philippine citizenship?
items: Naturalization (as an alien would)
Repatriation (RA 965, RA 2630, PD 725, RA 8171)
Direct act of Congress
Oath of allegiance under RA 9225 (for natural-born Filipinos naturalized abroad)
src: CA 63, Sec. 2; Bengson v. Cruz; RA 9225

title: Who may be repatriated
ask: Repatriation is available to those who lost citizenship through which five causes (Bengson)?
items: Desertion of the armed forces
Service in the armed forces of the Allied Forces in World War II (RA 965)
Service in the US armed forces at any other time (RA 2630)
Marriage of a Filipino woman to an alien (RA 8171; PD 725)
Political and economic necessity, for natural-born Filipinos (RA 8171)
src: Bengson III v. Cruz (2001); Angat v. Republic

title: Repatriation: how done and its effects
ask: How is repatriation done, where, and what are its effects?
items: Take the oath of allegiance to the Republic
Register it with the local civil registry (and the Bureau of Immigration under RA 8171)
File with the Special Committee on Naturalization, not the RTC (Angat)
Restores the original status: a natural-born Filipino is again natural-born (Bengson)
Retroacts to the date of the application (Frivaldo)
For local office, citizenship is needed at proclamation or start of term (Frivaldo)
src: RA 8171, Sec. 2; Angat; Bengson; Frivaldo

title: Who cannot be repatriated under RA 8171
ask: Under RA 8171, which applicants cannot be repatriated?
items: Persons opposed to organized government or affiliated with groups upholding such doctrines
Persons defending or teaching the necessity or propriety of violence, personal assault or assassination
Persons convicted of crimes involving moral turpitude
Persons suffering from mental alienation or incurable contagious diseases
src: RA 8171, Sec. 1 (the DG reviewer attributes these to CA 63 in its Angat digest)

title: RA 9225: retention and reacquisition
ask: What does RA 9225 cover and what are its effects?
items: Retention: natural-born Filipinos naturalized abroad after the law took effect (2003)
Reacquisition: natural-born Filipinos naturalized abroad before it took effect
Both by taking the oath of allegiance to the Republic
Extends to unmarried children below 18 (legitimate, illegitimate or adopted)
Reacquisition restores natural-born status (David v. SET)
Constitutional: dual citizenship is not dual allegiance (Calilung)
src: RA 9225, Secs. 3–4; Calilung; David v. SET

title: RA 9225, Sec. 5: civil and political rights
ask: Under RA 9225, Sec. 5, what conditions attach to the political rights of those who retain or reacquire citizenship?
items: To vote: meet Art. V and the overseas voting law
Elective office: meet the office’s qualifications and, on filing the COC, make a personal sworn renunciation of all foreign citizenship
Appointive office: swear allegiance and renounce foreign citizenship before an authorized officer before assuming office
Practice of a profession: obtain a license or permit from the proper authority
No voting or office while running for or holding public office in the foreign country
No voting or office while serving as an officer in that country’s armed forces
src: RA 9225, Sec. 5

title: Dual-citizen candidates: case rules
ask: What rules govern candidates who reacquired citizenship under RA 9225?
items: Two steps: oath of allegiance, then a personal and sworn renunciation (Chua)
Renunciation must be sworn before an authorized officer; an unsworn one abroad fails (Sobejana-Condon)
Foreign law must be proved, not judicially noticed (Sobejana-Condon)
Using a foreign passport after renouncing recants the renunciation (Maquiling)
Winning the election does not cure ineligibility (Chua)
Dual citizens by birth need not renounce; filing the COC suffices (Gana-Carait)
Disqualified winner: vacancy filled by succession, not by the second placer (Mangudadatu, 2025)
src: Chua; Sobejana-Condon; Maquiling; Gana-Carait; Mangudadatu

title: Dual citizenship versus dual allegiance
ask: Contrast dual citizenship with dual allegiance.
items: Dual citizenship: involuntary, from concurrent laws of two States (e.g., jus soli and jus sanguinis)
Dual allegiance: a positive act of continued loyalty to another State
Art. IV, Sec. 5 targets dual allegiance, not dual citizenship
Defining and dealing with dual allegiance is for Congress, not courts or agencies (Calilung)
So the CSC cannot bar dual citizens by memorandum; only a law can
src: Art. IV, Sec. 5; Calilung v. Datumanong; Gana-Carait

title: Qualifications of voters (Art. V, Sec. 1)
ask: What are the qualifications to vote under Art. V, Sec. 1?
items: Citizen of the Philippines
Not otherwise disqualified by law
At least eighteen years of age
Resided in the Philippines for at least one year
Resided in the place where he proposes to vote for at least six months immediately preceding the election
src: Art. V, Sec. 1

title: Requirements that may not be imposed on suffrage
ask: What three kinds of requirement does Art. V, Sec. 1 forbid?
items: Literacy requirement
Property requirement
Other substantive requirement (a burden achieving no permissible State objective: Ceniza)
src: Art. V, Sec. 1; Ceniza v. COMELEC

title: Congress’s duties under Art. V, Sec. 2
ask: What must Congress provide under Art. V, Sec. 2?
items: A system for securing the secrecy and sanctity of the ballot
A system for absentee voting by qualified Filipinos abroad
A procedure for the disabled and the illiterates to vote without the assistance of other persons
Until then, they vote under existing laws and COMELEC rules protecting ballot secrecy
src: Art. V, Sec. 2

title: Who are disqualified to vote (RA 8189, Sec. 11)
ask: Who are disqualified from voting under RA 8189, Sec. 11?
items: Sentenced by final judgment to at least one year’s imprisonment, unless pardoned or amnestied
Convicted by final judgment of a crime of disloyalty (rebellion, sedition, firearms laws, national security), unless restored
In both cases, the right returns automatically five years after service of sentence
Insane or incompetent persons so declared by competent authority, until declared otherwise

title: Is a new condition on voting valid?
ask: What questions decide whether a new condition on voting is valid?
items: Is it a qualification or substantive requirement (test, fee, property)? Then invalid
Is it registration or procedure? Valid if reasonable (registration only determines qualifications)
If it burdens the right, apply strict scrutiny: compelling interest, least restrictive means (Kabataan)
Did the right body act within the law? COMELEC cannot cut short what Congress fixed (Palatino)
src: Art. V, Sec. 1; AKBAYAN; Kabataan; Palatino

title: Registration periods and COMELEC’s stand-by power
ask: What are the statutory registration cut-offs, and when may COMELEC fix other dates?
items: No registration within 120 days before a regular election (RA 8189, Sec. 8)
No registration within 90 days before a special election (RA 8189, Sec. 8)
COMELEC’s stand-by power (RA 8436, Sec. 28): only if pre-election acts cannot reasonably be held in time
COMELEC bears the burden of showing that necessity (Palatino)
Exclusion petitions barred within 100 days before a regular election (65 for special) (RA 8189, Sec. 35)
src: RA 8189, Secs. 8, 35; RA 8436, Sec. 28; AKBAYAN; Palatino

title: AKBAYAN versus Palatino
ask: How do AKBAYAN (2001) and Palatino (2009) differ?
items: AKBAYAN: special registration sought within the 120-day prohibitive period; denied
AKBAYAN: COMELEC showed unfinished pre-election work (precincts, BEIs, book of voters, voters’ list)
Palatino: COMELEC closed registration before the 120-day period began; extension was outside it
Palatino: COMELEC showed no necessity; deadline voided and registration extended
Both: registration is valid procedural regulation under police power, not a qualification
src: AKBAYAN-Youth v. COMELEC; Palatino v. COMELEC

title: Why biometrics validation is valid (Kabataan)
ask: Why did Kabataan uphold biometrics validation under RA 10367?
items: It is part of registration, a procedural step, not a qualification or substantive requirement
Compelling interest: a clean voters’ list free of fraud reflecting the people’s will
Least restrictive means: validation done once while one stays an active voter
Deactivated voters may still apply for reactivation
src: Kabataan Party-List v. COMELEC (2015)

title: Ceniza: excluding HUC voters from provincial elections
ask: Why was excluding highly urbanized city voters from provincial elections valid (Ceniza)?
items: HUCs are independent of the province; loss of the provincial vote goes with independence
Income is a substantial distinction: it shows capacity to exist and develop independently
No constitutional right to vote for officials of a unit that does not govern you
Not a substantive requirement: no added burden on voters
Art. X, Sec. 12 (1987): HUC voters, and those of cities whose charters bar it, skip provincial elections
src: Ceniza v. COMELEC (1980); Art. X, Sec. 12

title: Overseas voting: who votes and for what (RA 10590)
ask: Under RA 10590, who may vote abroad and for which positions?
items: Citizens of the Philippines abroad, not otherwise disqualified by law
At least 18 years old on election day
Positions: President, Vice President, Senators, party-list representatives
Also all national referenda and plebiscites
src: RA 9189, as amended by RA 10590, Sec. 4

title: Overseas voting disqualifications (RA 10590)
ask: Who are disqualified from overseas voting under RA 10590?
items: Those who lost Philippine citizenship under Philippine law
Those who expressly renounced citizenship and pledged allegiance abroad, except RA 9225 retainers/reacquirers
Those finally convicted of an offense punishable by at least one year, unless pardoned; right returns after five years
Those declared insane or incompetent by competent authority, here or abroad
RA 10590 dropped RA 9189’s immigrant/permanent-resident bar and its three-year return affidavit
src: RA 10590, Sec. 5 (amending RA 9189)

title: Macalintal (2003): rulings on overseas absentee voting
ask: What did Macalintal v. COMELEC (2003) rule on RA 9189?
items: Overseas absentee voting is an exception to the residence requirement (necessary implication of Art. V, Sec. 2)
The affidavit of intent to return is valid: it shows domicile was never abandoned
A Joint Congressional Oversight Committee approving COMELEC’s rules is void: COMELEC’s independence
COMELEC cannot canvass and proclaim the President and VP; Congress does (Art. VII, Sec. 4)
src: Macalintal v. COMELEC (2003)

title: Requisites for a new domicile of choice
ask: What must concur to acquire a new domicile of choice?
items: Residence or bodily presence in the new locality
Intention to remain there (animus manendi)
Intention to abandon the old domicile (animus non revertendi)
The change must be voluntary (Romualdez)
src: Gallego v. Verra (1941); Romualdez v. RTC (1993)

title: Rules on residence in election law
ask: State the rules on residence (domicile) in election law.
items: Residence means domicile: a fixed residence to which, when absent, one intends to return (animus revertendi)
The domicile of origin is kept until a new one is acquired
Change is not presumed; whoever alleges it must prove all the elements
Absence for work or study does not lose domicile, even registering and voting elsewhere (Gallego)
Forced exile or flight for safety is not abandonment (Romualdez)
Same rule for candidates; an incumbent still serving cannot claim a new domicile (Mangudadatu)
src: Gallego; Romualdez; Co v. HRET; Mangudadatu

title: Two senses of ‘government’ (U.S. v. Dorr)
ask: In what two senses may ‘government’ be understood (Dorr), and which one does sedition law protect?
items: Abstract sense: the aggregate of institutions by which a society makes and carries out its rules
Administration: the aggregate of individuals who, for the time being, run the government
Sedition law protects the system (abstract sense), not the officials
Attacking officials’ character is not an attack on the government
src: U.S. v. Dorr (1903)

title: ‘Government of the Philippines’ (Admin. Code, Sec. 2(1))
ask: How does the Administrative Code define the ‘Government of the Republic of the Philippines’, and what arms does it include?
items: The corporate governmental entity through which governmental functions are exercised throughout the Philippines
Includes the arms through which political authority is made effective in the autonomous regions
… in the provincial, city, municipal or barangay subdivisions
… and in other forms of local government
src: Admin. Code (EO 292), Introductory Provisions, Sec. 2(1)

title: Constituent functions of government
ask: What are the constituent (compulsory) functions of government?
items: Keeping order and protecting persons and property from violence and robbery
Fixing legal relations between spouses and between parents and children
Regulating the holding, transmission and interchange of property
Determining contract rights and liabilities
Defining and punishing crime
Administering justice in civil cases
Determining political duties, privileges and relations of citizens
Dealing with foreign powers: security and international interests
src: Bacani v. NACOCO (1956), quoting Wilson; see ACCFA v. CUGCO

title: Ministrant functions and the modern view
ask: What are ministrant functions, with examples, and does the distinction still control?
items: Ministrant: optional functions to advance general welfare, not to keep society together
Examples: public works, public education, public charity
Examples: health and safety regulation, regulation of trade and industry
Modern view: distinction no longer controlling given the social justice mandate (ACCFA v. CUGCO)
src: Bacani v. NACOCO; ACCFA v. CUGCO (1969)

title: Governmental versus proprietary functions
ask: Contrast governmental and proprietary functions (Laurel v. Desierto).
items: Governmental: advance public welfare and carry out sovereign duties under a State policy
Proprietary: serve only a local or special community benefit, with no State policy involved
Examples: promoting culture and heritage (governmental) vs. a town fiesta (proprietary)
Why it matters: whether a post is a public office, and whether the entity is suable or liable
src: Laurel v. Desierto (2002)

title: Elements of a public office (Mechem)
ask: What are the five elements of a public office (Mechem, as applied in Laurel), and what is not essential?
items: Created by the Constitution, by the Legislature, or by a body acting under legislative authority
Delegated a portion of the sovereign powers of government, to be exercised for the public benefit
Powers and duties defined, directly or impliedly, by the Legislature or through legislative authority
Duties performed independently, without control of a superior other than the law (unless a subordinate office)
Some permanency and continuity, not merely temporary or occasional
Not essential: compensation; an honorary or temporary post may still be a public office (Laurel)
src: Laurel v. Desierto (2002), citing Mechem

title: De jure versus de facto government
ask: Contrast a de jure and a de facto government.
items: De jure: placed in power according to the constitution and laws (of right)
De facto: exists in fact without legal title, but must be accepted for practical purposes
A de facto government must be obeyed in civil matters while it lasts
Its acts not of a political complexion stay valid after the de jure government returns (postliminy)
Its political acts fall with it
src: Co Kim Cham v. Valdez Tan Keh (1945)

title: Three kinds of de facto government
ask: What are the three kinds of de facto government (Co Kim Cham)?
items: Usurpation: seizes control from the legitimate government by force or the majority’s voice and holds it
Paramount force: set up by military forces invading and occupying enemy territory in war (e.g., the Japanese-sponsored Republic)
Secession: set up as an independent government by inhabitants who rise in insurrection against the parent State
src: Co Kim Cham v. Valdez Tan Keh (1945)

title: Occupation rules in Co Kim Cham
ask: What rules on belligerent occupation did Co Kim Cham apply?
items: The occupant may suspend laws and promulgate new ones
It must respect municipal laws on public order and commerce, which continue so far as compatible (Hague Regulations)
A civil administration set up by the occupant is still a government of paramount force
Judicial acts not of a political complexion remain valid after liberation (postliminy)
MacArthur’s proclamation voiding ‘processes’ did not reach judicial processes
Restored courts may continue pending cases without an enabling law
src: Co Kim Cham v. Valdez Tan Keh (1945)

title: Revolutionary government (Republic v. Sandiganbayan)
ask: What are the rules on the Aquino revolutionary government, and the conditions for its directives to be valid?
items: Revolutionary because EDSA defied the 1973 Constitution after the Batasan proclaimed Marcos
Bound by no constitution: no Bill of Rights during the interregnum (Feb. 25, 1986 to the Freedom Constitution)
Still bound, as the de jure government, by the ICCPR and the Universal Declaration
Condition 1 for valid directives: enforcers did not exceed the authority granted by the revolutionary government
Condition 2: the directives did not violate the Covenant or the Declaration
Seizing items not named in the warrant failed both conditions
src: Republic v. Sandiganbayan (Ramas-Dimaano) (2003)

title: Why a sitting President cannot declare a revolutionary government
ask: Why can a sitting President not declare a revolutionary government?
items: He was elected under, and holds office by virtue of, the 1987 Constitution
Declaring one repudiates the Constitution and with it his own title to office
Nothing in the Constitution authorizes it
He cannot revolt against a government he himself heads (DG)
src: Republic v. Sandiganbayan; DG reviewer Q&A

title: Parens patriae: principles
ask: State the principles of parens patriae (SPARK).
items: The State acts as guardian of those who cannot protect themselves: minors, the mentally ill, incompetents, elderly, disabled
It supplements, not supplants, the parents’ primary right to rear their children
Restrictions on minors’ fundamental rights get strict scrutiny: compelling interest plus least restrictive means
It is not a grant of power to detain: the President needs a statute to detain loitering minors
src: SPARK v. Quezon City (2017); DG reviewer

title: Why minors may be treated differently
ask: What three justifications allow minors to be treated differently from adults (SPARK)?
items: The peculiar vulnerability of children
Their inability to make critical decisions in an informed and mature manner
The importance of the parental role in child rearing
src: SPARK v. Quezon City (2017), citing Bellotti v. Baird

title: SPARK: which curfews survived
ask: In SPARK, which curfew ordinances fell or survived, and why?
items: Compelling interest present: children’s welfare and protection from harm at night
Manila and Navotas failed least restrictive means: exceptions ignored association, religion, assembly, expression
Manila’s fines and imprisonment of minors conflict with the Juvenile Justice Act (status offenses)
Navotas’s community service sanction is valid
Quezon City upheld: its exceptions were narrowly drawn
src: SPARK v. Quezon City (2017)

title: State immunity: order of analysis
ask: In what order do you analyze a state immunity problem?
items: Is it really a suit against the State?
If so, has the State consented (expressly or impliedly)?
If a foreign State or agent: is the act jure imperii, and was the agent within official functions?
Even if suable: is the State liable, and how is a judgment paid (COA, no garnishment)?
src: Art. XVI, Sec. 3; PASI; GTZ; Minucher; Fetalvero

title: When a suit against an officer is a suit against the State
ask: When is a suit against a public officer really a suit against the State?
items: The officer is sued for acts done in the performance of official functions
A judgment would charge the treasury or create financial liability for the State
Or would require the State to perform an affirmative act (e.g., appropriate funds) (Arigo)
Formal impleading of the State is unnecessary
src: PASI v. Trinidad-Lichauco (2006); Arigo v. Swift (2014)

title: Exceptions: suit against officer is NOT against the State
ask: When is a suit against a public officer not a suit against the State (PASI)?
items: The officer acted beyond authority, illegally, or ultra vires: unauthorized acts are not State acts
Relief only nullifies the act, with no charge on the treasury
The government no longer has an interest to protect in the outcome
The officer is sued personally for a tort committed in performing duties
Obiter: adding damages on the nullity claims, or impleading the DOTC, would make it a suit against the State
src: PASI v. Trinidad-Lichauco (2006)

title: Forms of State consent to be sued
ask: In what forms may the State consent to be sued?
items: Express: by a general law
Express: by a special law
Implied: when the State itself sues (it opens itself to counterclaims)
Implied: when it enters into a commercial (jure gestionis) contract
Incorporated agency: its charter or the general law (‘sue and be sued’) controls, whatever its functions (GTZ)
Equity: immunity cannot avoid paying for a completed public work the State used (Vigilar)
src: Art. XVI, Sec. 3; Admin. Code, Book I, Sec. 10; GTZ; Vigilar

title: Suability versus liability and payment
ask: Once the State is suable, what limits remain on liability and payment?
items: Suability is not liability: consent to be sued is not admission of liability
Public funds cannot be garnished or levied on, even if appropriated (Fetalvero)
A money claim on a judgment goes to COA, which has primary jurisdiction
The State is bound only by acts of authorized agents done according to law (Admin. Code, Sec. 11(1))
The State is not bound by its officers’ mistakes or errors (Sec. 11(2))
Recovery on quantum meruit when the State benefited from a void contract (Vigilar)
src: Republic v. Fetalvero (2019); Vigilar v. Aquino (2011); Admin. Code, Book I, Sec. 11

title: Immunity of foreign States
ask: What rules govern the immunity of foreign States in Philippine courts?
items: Par in parem non habet imperium: equals have no jurisdiction over each other
Restrictive doctrine: immune for sovereign acts (jure imperii), not commercial acts (jure gestionis)
Suing officers where judgment needs foreign remedial acts or appropriations is suing the State (Arigo)
Warships are immune; the flag State bears international responsibility under UNCLOS (Arigo)
An implementing agency must prove immunity, e.g., by DFA certification; incorporated ones follow their charter (GTZ)
src: Arigo v. Swift; GTZ v. CA; Minucher

title: When a foreign agent shares State immunity (Minucher)
ask: When does a foreign agent share his State’s immunity, and when not?
items: He acted within his official functions, under the sending State’s directives
The host State consented to those activities (shown by official exchanges and joint operations)
Not immune when sued personally for acts beyond his functions, contrary to law and injurious to others
src: Minucher v. CA (2003)

title: Diplomatic immunity
ask: Who has diplomatic immunity, and how does it differ from State immunity (Minucher)?
items: Only diplomatic agents (heads of mission and diplomatic staff) have blanket civil and criminal immunity
Yardstick: whether the person performs duties of a diplomatic nature
Attachés who only assist the chief of mission are not diplomatic agents
Conferring diplomatic status is an Executive prerogative, not judicial
State immunity is broader: it covers any agent’s official acts done with host-State consent
src: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations; Minucher v. CA

title: Classes of heads of diplomatic mission
ask: What are the three classes of heads of mission under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (Art. 14)?
items: Ambassadors or nuncios accredited to Heads of State (and other heads of equivalent rank)
Envoys, ministers and internuncios accredited to Heads of State
Chargés d’affaires accredited to Ministers for Foreign Affairs
src: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, Art. 14; DG reviewer

title: Police power: definition and nature
ask: Define police power and state its essential characteristics.
items: Power to restrain liberty and property to promote the general welfare
Two elements: an imposition on liberty or property, to foster the common good
Inherent: needs no constitutional grant; born of statehood and sovereignty
The most pervasive of the inherent powers; implied limit on the Bill of Rights
Lodged in Congress; delegable to the President, agencies and LGUs (general welfare clause)
Executive use needs a statute passing the completeness and sufficient-standard tests (Zabal dissent)
src: Ermita-Malate; Rubi; Zabal; DG reviewer

title: Test of a valid exercise of police power
ask: What are the two requisites of a valid exercise of police power?
items: Lawful subject: the interests of the public generally, not a particular class, require the interference
Lawful means: reasonably necessary to accomplish the purpose and not unduly oppressive on individuals
src: U.S. v. Toribio; White Light; Zabal; DG reviewer
hook: Subject + means: right reason, right method

title: Requisites of a valid ordinance
ask: What are the requisites of a valid LGU ordinance (police power by LGUs)?
items: Must not contravene the Constitution or any statute
Must not be unfair or oppressive
Must not be partial or discriminatory
Must not prohibit, but may regulate, trade (Cruz v. Paras)
Must be general and consistent with public policy
Must not be unreasonable (White Light)
Must be within the power delegated to the LGU
src: Tatel v. Virac; Magtajas v. Pryce; Cruz v. Paras; White Light

title: Police power: upheld or struck down
ask: Which police power measures in the syllabus were upheld and which struck down?
items: Upheld: Mangyan reservation (Rubi, 1919) — read critically
Upheld: early warning devices on vehicles (Agustin v. Edu)
Upheld: six-month Boracay closure (Zabal)
Upheld: expanding MORE Power’s franchise into cooperatives’ areas (Iloilo I, 2024)
Struck down: ban on short-time motel rates (White Light)
Struck down: Manila and Navotas curfews (SPARK)
Struck down: ordinance closing all night clubs (Cruz v. Paras)
src: Rubi; Agustin; Zabal; Iloilo I; White Light; SPARK; Cruz v. Paras

title: Zabal: why the Boracay closure was valid
ask: Why did the majority in Zabal uphold the Boracay closure?
items: Lawful subject: a balanced and healthful ecology and public health
Lawful means: six months was reasonable for major, permanent rehabilitation works
The works could not be done with tourists on the island
The effect on travel was only incidental
Workers’ livelihood expectancies yield to the general welfare
No intrusion on local autonomy
src: Zabal v. Duterte (2019)

title: State-of-calamity remedies (Zabal dissent)
ask: What remedies does RA 10121, Sec. 17 allow on a state of calamity (the Zabal dissent’s point)?
items: Price ceiling on basic necessities and prime commodities
Monitoring and prevention of overpricing and hoarding
Programming or reprogramming of funds for repair of public infrastructure
Granting of no-interest loans to the most affected
Dissent: none of these authorizes closing an entire island
src: RA 10121, Sec. 17; Zabal v. Duterte (dissent)

title: Iloilo I: franchises yield to police power
ask: Why did Iloilo I uphold the expansion of MORE Power’s franchise, and what did the dissent say?
items: No franchise is exclusive (Art. XII, Sec. 11)
Franchises are subject to amendment, alteration or repeal by Congress when the common good requires
A franchise is a privilege, not the franchisee’s private property
As a grant, it is beyond the non-impairment clause; contracts yield to police power (Carlos Superdrug)
Leonen dissent: distribution is a natural monopoly; Art. XII, Sec. 19 allows regulating monopolies
Dissent: amendment must serve the common good, not competition alone
src: Iloilo I Electric Coop. v. Executive Secretary (2024)

title: Regulation or taking?
ask: When does a regulation become a taking, and how were the classic cases classified?
items: Rule: a taking appropriates property or its beneficial use for the public; regulation restrains a harmful use
Ericta (1983): 6% of cemetery land for paupers — taking without compensation, void
PPI v. COMELEC (1995): free print space for COMELEC — taking; must be paid
TELEBAP (1998): free airtime for COMELEC — valid; franchise over airwaves, a public resource
Manila Memorial (2013): senior and PWD discounts as tax deductions — valid police power
src: City Govt. of QC v. Ericta; PPI v. COMELEC; TELEBAP v. COMELEC; Manila Memorial v. DSWD

title: Police power, eminent domain and taxation compared
ask: Contrast the three inherent powers.
items: Purpose: regulate for general welfare / take property for public use / raise revenue
Compensation: none (general welfare) / just compensation / protection and public benefits
Property: use restrained, not taken / property or its use appropriated / money taken
All three are inherent: they exist without a constitutional grant; the Constitution only limits them
All three are lodged in Congress and may be delegated (e.g., to LGUs)
src: DG reviewer; Ericta; PPI

title: Limits on eminent domain
ask: What two requirements limit the power of eminent domain (Art. III, Sec. 9)?
items: Eminent domain requirement 1: taking for a particular public purpose (public use)
Eminent domain requirement 2: payment of just compensation to the owner
src: Republic v. Heirs of Borbon (2015); DG reviewer
